Kainos Group plc · KNOS-GB · Investment memo

Kainos: the market has paid for the revenue step-up, but the margin step-up is unforecast, modest and late, and one payer holds the downside

13 November 2026. Share price 1090p (close 11 November); market value about £1.3bn.

Fiscal years end 31 March (FY2027 is the year to 31 March 2027). Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model; figures marked "my" are my own estimates. Full conventions are in the end notes.

0. Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case. Kainos has delivered the revenue half of an earnings step-up, and the market has paid for it. The margin half has not started. The company has published how the margin will rise, it has carried out the same staffing change once before, and no broker has the margin rise in its estimates. If the margin rise arrives, earnings per share (EPS) grow about 15% a year for three years while revenue growth halves, and FY2029 EPS comes out 6% to 8% above consensus. But the margin rise arrives late: the first hard evidence is due in November 2027 and the proof in May 2028. Before then, Kainos's public-sector revenue has to pass through a UK fiscal calendar that could interrupt it.

What Kainos does. Kainos has three divisions. Digital Services builds and runs digital services for UK government and the National Health Service (NHS), about 60% of revenue. Workday Services implements Workday's HR and finance software for large employers, about 22%. Workday Products sells Kainos's own software to Workday customers, about 18%.

What matters most.

  1. Revenue is known, so the margin is the whole debate. Within three days of the interim results, consensus FY2028 revenue moved to the model's figure of £607m, and consensus puts a flat margin on that revenue. The entire difference between our forecasts and the market's is whether the margin rises: the model's EBITDA is 4% to 5% above consensus in FY2028 and 7% to 8% above in FY2029.
  2. The slowdown in growth that the market fears is what releases the margin. Management staffs growth above 20% with contractors and partners, who earn a quarter to two-thirds of the gross margin that Kainos's own staff earn. Digital Services growth will drop below 20% in H1 FY2028 for arithmetical reasons, because it is compared with a half that grew 57%. As growth slows, contractors leave and the margin recovers, so profit growth can hold near 15% while revenue growth falls to about 10%.
  3. The next six months lean slightly the wrong way. No event scheduled before May 2027 can show the margin turning, and Kainos's second-half margin has been below its first-half margin in each of the last six years. I have trimmed the model's FY2027 margin so that the year lands on consensus, not above it (topic 6).
  4. The downside comes from one payer and three dated events. NHS England is abolished in April 2027, a Spending Review with a large funding gap to close falls in autumn 2027, and an early general election is possible. I put about a one-in-five chance on a pause in public-sector work that cuts FY2028 EPS by 20% to 35% for one year. Past pauses have deferred work and have not cancelled it.
  5. Workday Products adds more to revenue visibility than to group margin, and its growth story runs ahead of its evidence. Products' contribution margin is only five points above Digital Services', so a richer software mix barely moves group margin. The real profit lever is Products' revenue outgrowing its own largely fixed cost base, which Kainos has yet to demonstrate.
  6. The return is good on earnings alone and extraordinary only at the guideline multiple. At a 32.2x fair multiple, a level the shares last reached in March 2022, the model shows +122% to its 18-month column and +171% to its three-year column. Two-thirds to three-quarters of that return is re-rating. What our research supports directly is the earnings: roughly +27% to +35% over 18 months at today's multiple if the forecasts are delivered, and about +13% once the flat-margin and pause cases are weighted in (my arithmetic, topic 12).

The skew. The outcomes are moderately skewed to the positive for FY2029 and beyond, and are not skewed to the positive for the next six months. Kainos is a sound case with a late catalyst. It becomes an unusually skewed case if any one of three things happens:

  • the contractor count is shown to have peaked (first hard reading in May 2027);
  • management commits to a group margin framework; or
  • the 2027 fiscal dates pass without an interruption to public-sector work.

The four judgements that move the shares (arithmetic in topic 9).

1. Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Evidence. UK public-sector digital demand has gone from trough to surge in eighteen months, and the surge is market-wide. Kainos's Digital Services revenue rose 57% in H1 FY2027 (public sector +55%, healthcare +85%, defence +44%). In comparable periods TPXimpact grew 60%, Netcompany's UK business about 50% and Capgemini's UK and Ireland business 25%.

Government contract awards have changed in kind as well as in number. Where government used to buy small projects, it now lets multi-year programmes such as that of the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA), worth £150m over five years. Policy supports the volume. Departmental budgets are set to 2028-29, and from January 2027 procurement scoring doubles the weight on social value to 20% and adds a definition of a UK supplier, both of which favour an onshore specialist such as Kainos.

The headwinds act on price and on billable hours. Global IT integrators underbid public work by 5% to 10% when their commercial work is slow. Workday's partner count in the UK and the rest of Europe, the Middle East and Africa has almost doubled, from 60 to 114, and Workday's own deployment automation is taking about 30% of the hours out of a standard implementation. About 60% of Kainos's revenue is still billed by time, so fewer hours per project mean less revenue per project.

The fiscal backdrop tightens inside the forecast period, on dated triggers. Real growth in departmental day-to-day spending slows from 2.8% in 2026-27 to 0.5% in 2027-28. The next Spending Review has been pushed to autumn 2027 and has a gap of £25bn to £40bn to close. NHS England is to be abolished and folded into the Department of Health by April 2027. An early general election is being discussed, although prediction markets in October put only a 25% chance on a vote by mid-2027.

Inference. The tailwinds are landing on volume and contract length, and the headwinds on price. The environment therefore underwrites Kainos's revenue for about two years and gives nothing to its margin. The trend in demand is still upward. The change in trend to watch is the fiscal tightening, and its triggers have dates.

So what. FY2027 and FY2028 revenue can be treated as backed by demand. Services prices should be assumed flat at best. Any margin gain has to come from Kainos's own decisions (topic 2).

Counter-case. A fiscal squeeze would turn the demand tailwind off. More than half of group revenue depends on UK public budgets, and after the 2024 election Kainos's public-sector revenue fell 15% in a half and profit expectations were cut by 20%. Two facts limit this risk. First, digital programmes are how departments deliver their savings (moving services online saves government about £1.75bn a year), so they are among the last items cut. Second, every past pause has deferred work rather than cancelled it: six to nine months in 2015, six weeks around the 2019 election, and two halves in 2024, when Kainos's healthcare revenue still grew 16%.

What would change my view. For the worse: the Home Office (£111m) and Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO, £84m) contracts still unsigned at 31 March 2027; any company statement that call-offs under existing contracts are slowing; or gross margin on Kainos's employee-delivered work falling below 38%, which would show that price competition has reached Kainos's own delivery. For the better: a recovery in commercial IT demand that pulls the integrators' spare capacity back out of public bids.

Versus the market. I agree with the market on demand, which is in every estimate. I differ from the market on the fiscal risk, in both directions. The market narrative treats the fiscal risk as generic: no broker we can see has connected the autumn 2027 Spending Review or the abolition of NHS England to Kainos's FY2028, and I treat both as dated risks to that year. Against that, I am more relaxed than a bear about what a pause would mean, because the historical record is one of deferral, not cancellation.

Conclusion. The environment gives Kainos a strong, contracted volume tailwind and no help on price, and its one real threat, the UK fiscal calendar, has dated triggers inside FY2028.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. UK public-sector digital demand has surged market-wide into multi-year programmes (Digital Services +57% in H1, budgets fixed to 2028-29, social-value and UK-supplier scoring favouring onshore specialists), giving a contracted volume tailwind for about two years on about 60% of revenue; but it gives nothing to price (integrators underbidding, Workday partners doubled, automation taking about 30% of implementation hours on the Workday side) and fiscal tightening (day-to-day real growth to 0.5%, an autumn 2027 Spending Review, NHS England abolition) trims it inside FY2028. Strong but partial and volume-only, consistent with the External group's 70: below Eckert & Ziegler's structural, less immediate tailwind and above Linea Directa's advanced cycle.

2. Internally driven change

Evidence. The founder, Brendan Mooney, returned as chief executive in December 2024 with about 9% of the shares. He cut 190 roles within three months, reset the strategy within ten months, hired a software leadership team for Workday Products from outside the company, and in August 2026 raised guidance in an unscheduled update.

The internal change that matters now is narrower: how Digital Services work is staffed. In H1 FY2027 Kainos earned a 39.0% gross margin on Digital Services work delivered by its own employees, 24.9% on work delivered by contractors and 9.6% on work passed through partners. Contractors and partners together delivered about 30% of the division's revenue. Management has published where it wants this staffing mix to settle: contractor spend at 5% and partner spend at 12% of revenue, which I read as Digital Services revenue. Management has made this change before, taking contractors from 209 to 42 during FY2024.

Kainos's current problems share one cause: growth outran delivery capacity. Contractors went from 69 to 316 in eighteen months. Workday Services ran at 73% utilisation while Digital Services was buying in contractors, so the group carried idle staff in one division and expensive capacity in another. A promise made in May 2026 of "clear margin improvement" in the second half of FY2027 became, in November, a condition: contractors stay while Digital Services grows faster than 20%.

Inference. The founder's reset and the demand recovery showed up in the same results, so revenue growth cannot show which of the two caused it. The margin can, because only the company's own choices move the margin. The margin is therefore the test of whether the internal change is real. So far, the internal change has produced revenue growth without any gain in margin.

So what. The margin lever is identified, sized and in management's hands. Reaching the staffing target is worth about 3 points of Digital Services gross margin on the company's figure; my arithmetic from the three margins above gives 2.8 points. On FY2028 divisional revenue of £367m, 2.8 points is about £10m of gross profit. After the training, holiday and bench costs that employees carry and contractors do not, it is about £6m of PBT, or 4p of EPS (6%). On my reading of the model's segment build, the model banks almost none of this gain in FY2028, about 40% by FY2029 and about three-quarters by FY2030. Consensus banks none of it.

Counter-case. Contractor dependence is structural. Public programmes must be staffed in weeks, and a contractor deploys in four weeks where a permanent hire takes five months. Management itself classes 40% of the increase in partner work as permanent, the price of being prime contractor. Two programmes of about £100m each mobilise in FY2028, just as DEFRA's surge capacity should be leaving. A close peer, Made Tech, tried the same conversion in 2022-23 and saw utilisation fall from 79% to 68% when client delays met an enlarged permanent bench.

What would change my view. For the worse: more than about 350 contractors at March 2027, or any mention of new surge capacity for the Home Office and FCDO programmes; or a second share sale by a director's family, after the £5.9m sale by the finance director's family in July 2026. For the better: a contractor count that has peaked by May 2027, and above all a stated group margin target, which I put at about a one-in-four chance within 18 months.

Versus the market. The market read the 9 November interim results as "growth without operating gearing" and took 12% off the shares. I agree with that reading for the next two reporting dates. I differ on FY2029: the staffing mechanism is published, has a precedent and is absent from every estimate we can see.

Conclusion. The internal change is real and has produced the revenue, and the company has now named the one lever that would turn revenue into margin, the staffing mix, without yet pulling it.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. The founder's return (190 roles cut, strategy reset, outside software leadership, an unscheduled guidance raise) is real, and he has named, sized and once delivered the staffing lever (contractors 209 to 42 in FY2024), worth about 3 points of Digital Services gross margin or about 6% of EPS, mostly from FY2029; but so far the change has produced revenue the external surge would largely have brought anyway, with contractors up to 316, net promoter score down from 70 to 61, Products margins diluted by loss-making installs and the H2 margin promise withdrawn. A funded, credible but not-yet-pulled lever net of present capacity problems is an offset positive in the low 60s, a little below the Internal group's 66 because I credit the revenue to topic 1: below OEM's working acquisition engine and above Odfjell's largely external margin gain.

3. Value chain, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Evidence and inference. The industry gives Kainos plentiful demand and little protection on price. Services markets are fragmented and easy to enter, and competitors chase volume: when Kainos refused to discount, its share of the main government digital framework fell from about 10% to 4.6% in two years. Kainos's advantages are specific to the niches it has chosen. Few suppliers can act as prime contractor on a £100m public programme. Kainos's complex, multi-country Workday deployments are winning more large deals (13 above $1m, against 7 a year earlier). And Kainos's software sits inside Workday's platform, with more than 750 customers, churn below 4% and 40% of customers on two or more products.

The best single piece of evidence that these positions hold is that the margin on Kainos's own employees' work was almost unchanged (39.0% against 39.5% a year earlier) through a period in which the industry's prices fell. The advantage is customer trust and switching cost: 82% of revenue comes from existing customers. That trust lets Kainos hold its price and walk away from underpriced work. It does not let Kainos raise its price.

Kainos's financial profile is above average on returns and cash and only average on margin. Return on equity is above 40%, there is no debt and there is £86.5m of cash, and free cash flow before dividends has been above net income in each of the last three years. (FactSet's free cash flow line deducts dividends and so understates this.) But PBT margin has fallen from 20.2% in FY2024 to 15.5%, and on FactSet's adjusted basis EPS was barely higher in FY2026 than in FY2021 (35.2p against 33.3p) while revenue rose 83%.

Management is a strong, aligned founder-operator who acts quickly. The blemishes are relevant ones: a succession that failed in 2023-24 and no named successor now, delivery capacity that was under-built for a recovery the founder himself predicted, and no stated margin ambition.

So what. Business quality supports confidence in revenue delivery and in fast cost action if demand falls. It does not support any assumption of pricing power. Two outside decision-makers hold most of the large risks. One is the Treasury. The other is Workday, which stands behind 44% of revenue, is the sole seller of one of Kainos's newest products, and in October 2026 launched its own software agents next to Kainos's two oldest and most profitable products.

Counter-case. Kainos's advantages are borrowed. Its demand is one government's budget, its software channel is one vendor's goodwill, and Viewforth's Wisdom Library classes Kainos as a "treadmill" that must keep winning and hiring, not a compounder. I accept most of this. What I hold against it is that both dependencies have been stable in direction for a decade and that the customer-level switching costs belong to Kainos itself.

What would change my view. Products recurring-revenue growth below 20%; any change to Workday's exclusive resale arrangement or its fixed fee; the share of revenue from existing customers falling below 80%; or the loss of a core framework at re-tender.

Versus the market. The market pays about a third more for Kainos than for its peers (17.4x two-year-forward earnings against about 13x), and brokers justify the premium with a software multiple on Products. I think the premium is earned by the returns, the cash and the growth. I think the Products part of the brokers' argument is weaker beyond 18 months than the narrative suggests. One popular fear I do not share: the break clause in the Workday agreement, first exercisable in August 2027, is Kainos's option, not Workday's, so that date is a non-event.

Conclusion. Kainos is a high-return, net-cash, founder-led business with real but moderate advantages that defend its price and never raise it, and two outside parties, the Treasury and Workday, hold the keys to its largest risks.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. Qualitatively ordinary-to-good: a fragmented, easy-entry, volume-first services industry with no pricing power (framework share fell from 10% to 4.6% when it refused to discount), real but niche advantages (prime-contractor scale, complex Workday deployments, Products with sub-4% churn) and an aligned founder-operator, but with two outside parties (the Treasury and Workday, behind 44% of revenue) holding the largest risks and no successor. The financial profile is strong on returns and cash (return on invested capital 34%, 97th percentile; return on equity 94th; net cash) but weak on margin (EBITDA margin 29th percentile, operating margin down 1.2 points over three years) and recent capital has earned little (incremental PBT margins of 2% and 13%, EPS flat FY2021-26 on 83% more revenue), so it sits well below Reply, the comparable IT-services anchor, about level with Helios Towers and below Carlsberg, coherent with groups of 40/47/70/70.

4. Guidance, expectations management and the delivery record

Evidence. Kainos gives no numerical guidance. It guides by reference to a consensus it compiles itself, and for FY2027 it says "in line". Its record splits cleanly. On revenue it beats: by 6% against consensus in FY2026 and by 5% against the most-cited broker in H1 FY2027. On profit it lands in line, as in FY2026, or slightly ahead, as in H1 FY2027. It has had one large miss in five years, the 20% profit cut that followed the 2024 election. Changes to guidance have come in unscheduled or early-autumn statements, once four to six months of the year were known: a cut in October 2024, and raises in September 2025 and August 2026.

Inference. Kainos under-promises on revenue and is exact on profit. The revenue cushion is now used up, because consensus absorbed it within days of the interim results. On margin, the present guidance is not conservative. "In line" for the year needs the second-half margin to roughly match the first-half margin, and on FactSet's basis the second half has fallen short of the first in each of the last six years: by 0.2 to 3.6 points in five of those years and by more in the restructuring year. Research written for this memo shows that the causes are structural. The June pay review lands fully in the second half, about 200 early-careers staff join in the autumn before they can be billed, and the second half has fewer working days.

The withdrawal of the margin promise has a constructive side. By withdrawing the second-half margin promise in November, management cleared margin expectations out of the estimates. The implied consensus EBITDA margin for FY2028 fell to 15.9%, the same as for FY2027. For FY2028 and FY2029, the bar on margin is now as low as it can reasonably be.

So what. Expect Kainos to say "in line" in the April 2027 trading update and again at the May 2027 results. Do not expect a raise before August to October 2027, which is when this company changes guidance. I have lowered the model's FY2027 margin so that the year lands on consensus PBT of about £84m, where the model had £85.2m (topic 6).

Counter-case. The company habitually sandbags its guidance, and at least one broker called the November guidance "highly conservative". The 11% increase in employees hired in the first half becomes billable in the second half, which could offset the seasonal costs.

What would change my view. An April trading update that says profit is ahead of consensus would restore the higher FY2027 figure and would be the earliest sign that the contractor count has peaked. A second-half PBT margin below 14.5% in May would lead me to cut FY2028.

Versus the market. The friendly reading is that Kainos's guidance is conservative across the board. I think that is true of revenue, where it no longer helps, and untrue of the second-half margin. I agree with the more cautious broker, Deutsche Bank, that FY2027 profit will be what the company says it will be.

Conclusion. Kainos reliably beats on revenue and delivers in line on profit, but its guidance cushion has been absorbed: expectations are conservative on margin for FY2028 and FY2029, and not for the half now under way.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. Kainos reliably beats on revenue (6% in FY2026, 5% in H1) and lands in line or slightly ahead on profit, with raises in September 2025 and August 2026, but within the window it cut profit expectations 20% in October 2024 and has just walked back its May 2026 promise of clear H2 margin improvement; current 'in line' guidance is not conservative on the H2 margin, which has fallen short of H1 in each of six years. A record like Renew's (a cut, then beats) with an added margin walk-back puts it just below Renew and above CVS, coherent with the Guidance and Sell-side groups (53/47).

5. What turns revenue growth into profit growth

Evidence. For five years, revenue growth did not turn into profit growth at Kainos: EPS was flat from FY2021 to FY2026 while revenue rose 83% (topic 3). The incremental PBT margin on new revenue was 2% in FY2026 and 13% in H1 FY2027, because growth was bought with contractors and partners. In the other direction, a 4% fall in revenue in FY2025 cut PBT by 15%.

Of the five levers that turn revenue into profit, only cost control is strong at Kainos.

Inference. Management's staffing rule works as a governor on profit. Above 20% growth, extra revenue arrives at contractor margins, so profit rises less than revenue. Below 20% growth, contractors leave and the margin recovers, so profit holds up as revenue slows. In moderate scenarios profit therefore varies less than revenue in both directions. The governor fails only in a pause, when the employed workforce, up about 19% in a year, becomes idle cost.

A second inference corrects a common belief that a richer software mix lifts group margin. Products' contribution margin after its own research and sales costs is 26.5%, against 21.5% for Digital Services. Moving one point of group revenue from Digital Services to Products therefore adds only about 0.05 points to group operating margin. A richer software mix lifts gross margin and does almost nothing for profit. What would lift profit is Products' revenue outgrowing Products' own largely fixed costs.

So what. The idea that revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth has been false at Kainos and has to become true for the case to work. The model has the incremental PBT margin at 22% in FY2028 and about 30% in FY2029 and FY2030. The route to that margin is slower growth and a different staffing mix. It is not price, and it is not software mix.

Counter-case. The governor is a polite description of a business that cannot earn operating leverage in an upswing and suffers negative operating leverage in a downswing. That has been true so far. The reply is that the forecast does not need the old margins back: it has Digital Services' contribution margin peaking below 23%, against a four-year average of 27%.

What would change my view. Two consecutive halves in which revenue growth is below 20% and the margin does not rise would mean that the margin dilution is structural.

Versus the market. The market treats the coming slowdown in revenue growth, from 27% in FY2027 to about 10%, as the bad news that follows a peak. I think the slowdown is the trigger for operating leverage, which is why I expect profit growth to hold near 15%. I also think the widely repeated view that software mix will re-rate group margins fails on the arithmetic above.

Conclusion. Kainos has no pricing power and little fixed-cost leverage, so outsized profit growth depends on one mechanism, the staffing mix, which management controls and which slower growth switches on.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Structurally the model has little gearing on the way up: no pricing power in services, only about 16% of costs fixed within a year, no financial leverage, and a staffing rule that staffs growth above 20% with contractors at a quarter to two-thirds of employee margin, so incremental PBT margins were 2% and 13%; the forecast EPS-to-revenue growth ratio (about 14% on about 8%, roughly 1.7x) is below the Universe's median 2x, while the downside bites (a 4% revenue fall cut PBT 15%). Strong cost-out scope (contractors releasable in weeks, the 2025 restructuring) and Products' revenue outgrowing its own largely fixed cost base lift it above the 25 level, but this is below the ordinary mix, and below the Economic strength group's 70, which rests on returns and cash rather than gearing.

6. Forecast financials

The forecasts of record (model update 2).

The FY2026 column is on the company's adjusted basis. The model's own summary shows FY2026 on FactSet's basis, so its "+50.7%" EPS growth for FY2027 mixes two bases and should not be quoted. Like for like, FY2027 EPS growth is about 30%.

Evidence and inference. The period ahead reverses the shape of the last five years. Then, revenue grew fast and EPS stood still. Now, revenue growth slows to 7% to 11% a year after FY2027, and EPS compounds at about 14% a year from FY2027 to FY2031, because PBT margin rises by nearly three points, from 15.5% to 18.3%. Double-digit EPS growth is forecast in every year. The PBT margin rises but never returns to FY2024's 20.2%, for three reasons: part of the partner work is permanent, Workday Services pricing keeps falling, and the increase in employer National Insurance contributions is permanent.

Where the margin gain comes from matters more than its size. Over the four years, about half of the gain is Products' revenue outgrowing Products' own cost base, about a fifth is the release of contractors, and the rest is central costs and mix. FY2028 is different, and reassuringly so. On my reading of the segment build, most of the FY2028 gain comes from two near-mechanical items. The first is Workday's fixed US$10m annual fee spread over 18% more Products revenue, which holds as long as Products' research and sales spending grows no faster than its revenue. The second is central costs growing 7% against revenue growing 10.6%. Contractor release contributes under £1m. The FY2028 forecast therefore leans little on the uncertain staffing lever; the FY2029 and FY2030 forecasts need it.

Cash follows earnings after a dip. Free cash flow is low in FY2027 because of about £28m of capital spending, most of it on the headquarters, and returns to roughly 100% of net income from FY2028.

My change to the inputs. I have lowered the EBITDA margin by 0.1 to 0.2 points a year to FY2030 and left FY2031 at 18.8%. The reason is the second-half seasonality in topic 4. The model had the second half of FY2027 slightly above the first half, and I have it 0.2 points below, at 15.6%. Because the seasonal costs recur, the lower base carries into the next two years with the same improvement steps. The effect is about 1% off EPS in each of FY2027 to FY2029. The gap to consensus EBITDA becomes about 4% in FY2028 and 7% in FY2029. All other figures in this memo are the model's, unchanged.

Counter-case. Deutsche Bank holds the PBT margin flat at 15.2% to 15.4% to FY2029, which gives EPS of 57.4p in FY2028 and 63.7p in FY2029, 6% and 10% below the model. Its reasoning is that early revenue outperformance seldom becomes profit upside in this industry, and three years of falling margin at Kainos support that reasoning.

What would change my view. Upwards: fewer than about 290 contractors at September 2027 with Digital Services still growing near 10%. Downwards: a failed second-half margin test (topic 4), or Products' gross margin failing to recover above 75.5% as new-product installations mature.

Versus the market. I agree with consensus on FY2027. For FY2028 the market has our revenue at a flat margin, and I have a modest margin rise that owes more to fixed costs than to contractors. For FY2029 I am above consensus on both revenue (by 4%) and margin. The difference between our forecasts and consensus comes down to one variable, the margin, and it is the variable the sell-side has just stopped forecasting.

Conclusion. The forecasts show EPS growing about 14% a year on slowing revenue. That reversal of the past five years is near-mechanical in FY2028, and from FY2029 it depends on the staffing mix and on Products' cost base.

Score: 79, set by the Rater. The growth is organic and double-digit in every year, against flat EPS over the past five, and runs near the top of the 10-15% band; I place it just above mid-band rather than higher because the margin only recovers part of the way (PBT margin 15.5% to 18.3%, never back to FY2024's 20.2%), about a tenth comes from buybacks, and the FY2029-30 steps depend on the unproven staffing and Products levers (consensus has about 12%).

7. Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Evidence. Kainos has up to four company statements in the next twelve months: a year-end trading update around 20 April 2027, full-year results in mid to late May 2027, a possible unscheduled update in August to October 2027, and interim results in November 2027. The milestones before May are well founded and already expected: recurring revenue from Products passing £100m in December, the two pending contracts signing, and the contracted backlog passing £1bn. The April update is normally a few sentences long. The May results give the first reading of contractor numbers since September and the first statement on FY2028. The November interims give contractor numbers and margins by type of staff for the first half in which Digital Services growth falls below the 20% staffing trigger.

Inference. Scope for upgrades over six months is close to nil. The revenue upgrades have already happened. Operating-profit estimates cannot rise until margin evidence exists, and the first margin evidence arrives in month six at the earliest and more probably in month twelve. Over six to twelve months the scope is real but conditional. My estimates for consensus operating profit for FY2028 and FY2029 are below. A raise would be worth about 4% on FY2028 EBITDA and 7% on FY2029, and it would fall mostly on FY2029, the year on which the shares will by then be valued. A cut, if it comes, would be larger: the 2024 precedent is 20% within weeks, from every broker at once.

So what. The narrative available to the market is that margin follows growth, and its proof points are dated, so the sequence of evidence matters more than the size of any single upgrade. Three smaller positives could arrive inside twelve months, and none is in anybody's numbers: a contractor count that has visibly peaked by May; a margin framework from management; and a restart of buybacks once the headquarters is finished in summer 2027, which the rebuild in net cash makes affordable.

Counter-case. The sell-side will follow and will not lead. The broker that sets the tone promised margin improvement from the second half of FY2027 in an April 2026 note, had to withdraw it, and now holds the margin flat for three years. Until that broker moves, good operating data may be met with "wait for the margin". And the next two events could bring a small negative: a soft second-half margin in May would be carried into FY2028 estimates.

What would change my view. A margin target, or a statement in May that contractor numbers are falling, would bring the upgrade window forward by six months. Slower call-offs ahead of the Spending Review would close the window.

Versus the market. The market expects continued revenue strength and a flat margin, and nothing in the next six months will surprise it on either. The market has not considered a weaker second half. It does not expect any margin recovery in FY2028, which is the one place where a positive surprise is available.

Conclusion. There is no scope for upgrades before May 2027, and a real but conditional scope from November 2027, worth about 4% on FY2028 and 7% on FY2029 operating profit.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, will be 'in line' in April and May and is unlikely to be raised before August-October 2027, and the seasonally weaker H2 margin leans the next reading slightly negative; the memo's odds on consensus operating profit over twelve months (raised about 30% by about 4-7%, held 45-50%, cut 20-25% with a 2024-style cut of up to 20%) net to roughly nil or slightly negative against about 10% revenue growth, around the Universe's 40th percentile. The real, conditional upside (contractor peak, a margin framework, buyback restart) lands mostly at or after month twelve, so it sits a little below Kerry and just above Tele2, coherent with the fourth-set group's 48.

8. Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Evidence. Kainos's momentum is strong on revenue estimates, price and UK peers, and weak on profit estimates and ratings.

Inference. Kainos's momentum is strong in level and fading in direction. The headline revision score (7, among the best in the sector) is driven by sales estimates. Beneath it, profit estimates have stopped moving, and after the interim results the implied margin went down. Strong price momentum combined with fading estimate momentum is the pattern of a completed first leg of a rally. The peer evidence says that Kainos's demand is real and shared with its UK peers, and that its premium rating is its own and not the sector's.

So what. Momentum will not carry the shares from here, and the next leg needs new information (topic 7). One positive detail: with the price a fifth below its high, some of the valuation-driven rating downgrades could reverse without any change in estimates.

Counter-case. The pause in the shares may be the start of a stall. The share price has fallen below its 50-day average, target prices are falling, and the stock moves one-for-one with its sector in sell-offs.

What would change my view. A fall through the rising 200-day average without company news would say that the market is pricing a sector or fiscal problem. FY2028 EBITDA estimates rising faster than sales estimates would say that the second leg has begun.

Versus the market. I agree with the dashboard's split verdict. Where I differ from a casual reading of the revision score is that I treat it as a sales-revision signal: the earnings momentum that matters, at the operating-profit line, is flat.

Conclusion. Momentum is good on revenue, price and UK peers and has stalled on operating profit, which is the pattern of a first leg that is complete.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Both measures are positive, three-month EPS revisions are +6% (83rd percentile) with guidance raised in August and held after a beat, and UK specialist peers are upgrading, so B; I place it at the floor of the band because the parts hold it back: Buy ratings down 44 points to 56%, targets slipping, the 50-day average lost and the price 20% off its high, and revisions driven by sales with EBITDA estimates barely moving after the results, though not strongly enough to cut the letter.

9. Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts

Simplicity. The case is simple. It has three drivers, each with a published measure: public-sector volume (bookings and backlog), the staffing mix (contractor numbers and margin by type of staff), and Products growth (recurring revenue). An outsider can rebuild EPS from the company's own disclosure, which is unusual for a services business. One point of group PBT margin is worth about £5.5m, or 3.5p of EPS.

The range of FY2028 outcomes (my estimates, on the model's basis).

FY2027 EPS is close to settled, at about 51.5p to 55p. For FY2028 the most likely outcome is a little above consensus, and the probability-weighted outcome, about 58p, is a little below it. The body of the range is tight and the lower tail is long. The earlier research put the chance of a pause at 15%. I have raised it to about one in five, because research on the election commissioned since then shows that the question is live, even though a snap election that returns the same government has historically cost weeks rather than half-years.

Fragilities.

  • The backlog is less contracted than its headline. Of the £600m Digital Services backlog on the new total-contract-value basis, only £219m (37%) is committed work orders, equal to seven or eight months of the division's revenue. The rest is awarded value that departments draw down through further orders, and the Treasury controls those further orders.
  • The employed workforce has been hired ahead of demand. The base case needs the workforce to keep growing into a slowing revenue line, which is the configuration that hurt Kainos in FY2025.
  • Information is infrequent. Kainos reports twice a year. Revenue can be followed from outside through contract award notices; the margin cannot.

Suddenness and the share price. Company news arrives on four known dates; fiscal and sector shocks arrive undated. On ordinary days the peer group explains under a quarter of the stock's moves, and in sector sell-offs about half. The company therefore sets the multiple on the way up and the sector sets it on the way down, and over 18 months the multiple is a larger source of variance than the earnings.

The precedents for sudden falls are specific. In October 2024 Kainos cut profit expectations by 20% after the election. Healthcare revenue fell 31% in a half when NHS Digital was merged into NHS England in 2023. TPXimpact issued a profit warning in September 2024, two months after a confident outlook. In early 2026 the shares fell to about 730p on sector fears about AI, during a run of good company news.

The four judgements, with the arithmetic. For FY2028 and FY2029, £1m of PBT is £0.735m after tax at 26.5%, or about 0.63p of EPS on 117m shares.

1. The margin turns in FY2028 and continues in FY2029. If it stays at FY2027's 15.9%, as consensus and Deutsche Bank assume:

  • FY2028: 0.8 points × £607m = £4.9m of PBT; after tax £3.6m; 3.0p of EPS. EPS falls from 61p to 58p (-5%) and free cash flow from £70m to about £66m.
  • FY2029: 1.8 points × £659m = £11.9m; after tax £8.7m; 7.4p. EPS falls from 71p to about 63.5p (-10%), which is Deutsche Bank's 63.7p.
  • If the turn comes half a year early: +0.4 points × £607m = £2.4m, or +1.5p in FY2028.
  • A rule of thumb: every 100 contractors replaced by employees is about £2m of gross profit, £1.2m of PBT after the costs employees carry, and 0.75p.
  • The upside from faster growth is capped. If Digital Services grew 20% in FY2028 and not 10%, the extra £33m of revenue would be staffed with contractors and would earn the 13% incremental margin seen in H1: £4.3m of PBT and +2.7p. Group revenue would be 5.5% higher and EPS 4.5% higher.

2. Public-sector work keeps flowing. The model has Digital Services revenue of £367m in FY2028.

  • One-half pause: revenue 5% below FY2027's £333.5m is £317m, a shortfall of £50m (8% of group revenue). Temporary contractors are assumed gone already, so the loss falls on employee-delivered work at a 39% gross margin with the staff still paid: £50m × 39% = £19.5m of PBT (-20%); after tax £14.3m; 12p. EPS is about 49p and free cash flow about £55m.
  • Two-half pause: a shortfall of £83m × about 40% = £33m of PBT (-34%); 21p. EPS is about 40p.
  • The response: a headcount cut of 7%, as in March 2025, removes £15m to £18m of annual cost, so the damage is a one-year event.

3. Workday Products compounds and begins to show operating leverage. The model has Products revenue growing 18% and 17% in FY2028 and FY2029, with contribution margin rising from 27% to 32.5% by FY2031. Suppose instead growth of 12% a year and a margin stuck at 27%, because Workday's own agents slow the two core products and each new launch keeps depressing margin.

  • FY2029: revenue £98.8m × 1.12² = £124m, against £136m. Contribution £124m × 27% = £33.5m, against £40.5m: £7m less PBT, 4.4p. EPS falls from 71p to about 66.5p (-6%).
  • FY2031: revenue £155m against £179m; contribution £42m against £58m: £16m less PBT (-12%), about 10.5p on 112m shares. EPS falls from 91p to about 80p.
  • The valuation effect comes sooner than the earnings effect. Deutsche Bank values Products at about 4.2 times sales. At 3 times, on about £118m of sales, the sum of the parts loses about £140m, or 120p a share (11%).

4. The market pays at least today's multiple. This judgement moves the price and leaves EPS unchanged. At 1090p the shares are on 17.4x consensus two-year-forward EPS of 62.6p, so each turn of the multiple is 63p, or 5.7%.

  • 14.5x (five-year 10th percentile): 908p, -17%.
  • 19.5x (five-year median): 1221p, +12%.
  • 24.1x (ten-year median): 1509p, +38%.
  • 32.2x (the guideline): 2017p, +85%.
  • A pause that also cut forward EPS to about 55p would give about 800p at 14.5x, -27%.

Counter-case. Calling the case "simple" understates the risk: there is no diversification across the three drivers, and each driver is controlled by one decision-maker. I accept that, and I describe the case as simple but not low-risk.

What would change my view. Passing April 2027 (the abolition of NHS England) and the autumn 2027 Spending Review without a slowdown would cut the lower tail roughly in half. A margin target would narrow the body of the range.

Versus the market. The brokers' FY2028 EPS range, 56.4p to 62.0p, covers the body of outcomes only: no published estimate contains a pause. The market's attention since 9 November has been on the margin. I think the larger risk to the share price is the fiscal tail and the sector multiple, and the larger opportunity is the margin.

Conclusion. The forecasts are simple and tight in the body, with a long lower tail that one payer controls, and the share price takes its downside from the sector and its upside from the company.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. The case is simple (three published, rebuildable drivers, net cash) and the FY2028 EPS body is tight (55% at 61-64p, 25% at about 58p), but a 20% chance of a public-sector pause cuts EPS 20-35% for a year, the tail is controlled by one payer with three dated triggers, the margin is seen only twice a year, and the multiple follows the sector down (the AI-fear drop to 730p in early 2026). Better than IMCD's levered, downgrade-ridden case and close to NKT's net-cash case with one concentrated sudden risk; a little below the Risks groups (55/60) because I weight the long tail and sector-driven multiple more.

10. Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Evidence. The shares bottomed twice, in March 2025 (664p, 14.3x forward earnings) and in March 2026 (730p, 12.8x). They turned up in spring 2026, re-rated in August on the guidance raise and reached 1360p in the autumn. That first leg ended on 9 November. Since then the fundamentals have kept broadening: bookings up 27%, more and larger programmes, Canada growing 50%, defence now reported separately, and Products recurring revenue up 24%. Operating-profit estimates have stopped rising, and the price has given back a fifth. The dashboard's rule places the stock in the Broadening phase.

Inference. I agree with the Broadening label, with one qualification. The thesis is broadening in revenue terms only: there are more sources of growth, at the same margin. The stock is pausing inside that phase. The next phase, Reinforcing, needs earnings to rise faster than revenue, and the evidence for that is due between November 2027 and May 2028. The phase that threatens is Stalling, which would follow if a soft second half and a fiscal interruption arrived together.

So what. The lifecycle phase argues for patience about timing more than for doubt about direction. A stock pausing after a completed first leg is usually driven by the next dated event, and for Kainos the next two dated events, the April trading update and the May results, are the least informative.

Counter-case. The pause is the top. A half of 57% growth will not be extrapolated, the margin promise has slipped once, an insider's family sold shares in July, and the description "priced for the revenue, not yet paid for the margin" may flatter a stock that simply got ahead of itself.

What would change my view. Towards Reinforcing: contractors falling and Digital Services gross margin rising at the November 2027 interims. Towards Stalling: a cut to FY2028 operating-profit estimates from any cause.

Versus the market. The price action since 9 November treats the story as stalled. I read it as a pause, because the fundamental data are still improving and the missing piece, margin evidence, has a date.

Conclusion. Kainos is in the Broadening phase on revenue and in a pause on earnings and price, and the move to Reinforcing depends on margin evidence that is twelve to eighteen months away.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The memo's Broadening is right for revenue (bookings +27%, Canada +50%, Products recurring revenue +24%) but the stock has completed its first leg and is pausing: operating-profit estimates have stopped rising, the price is a fifth below its high, and the move to Reinforcing needs margin evidence due November 2027 to May 2028, with the next two events the least informative; the computed Reinforcing overstates it. That is late Broadening with a paused, not stalled, earnings story, close to Nexans's paused Reinforcing and just above Greggs.

11. The fair multiple

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline sets the fair multiple for a stock in Broadening at the 80th percentile of its own ten-year range, which for Kainos is 32.2x two-year-forward earnings. The model's multiple today is 18.4x.

My view. The guideline's direction is right, but its level is too high for where this stock is. Four observations support that view.

  1. The 32.2x level comes from one unrepeatable period. Every month-end at or above 32.2x in the ten years falls between December 2019 and March 2022. Revenue growth was then peaking at about 30% a year and the operating margin at about 21%, and interest rates were close to zero.
  2. The market's recent ceiling is much lower. The multiple has not ended a month above 21x since August 2023. The high point of this year's re-rating, reached while estimates were rising about 10% in a quarter, was about 20x at a month-end and about 22x at the peak price.
  3. Kainos is at peak delivery in revenue only. The guideline reserves the upper part of the range for peak delivery phases. In earnings, the margin leg is still a forecast, the lower tail is long and the forecasts are less certain than the phase label implies. On the guideline's own logic, that argues for the middle of the range.
  4. The sector has been de-rated. Peers trade at about 13x, and the most-cited broker values Products by reference to Workday's own multiple, which is under pressure as Workday's growth slows.

I would treat 19x to 21x as fair while the margin is unproven. That range is centred on the five-year median (19.5x) and matches the multiple implied by the median broker target. I would treat about 24x, the ten-year median, as the realistic upside if the margin leg is delivered. Kainos traded at about 24x from mid-2017 to 2019, in a friendlier market, and a business growing EPS at 14% a year with net cash, returns on equity above 40% and full cash conversion can justify that multiple. I would treat 14.5x to 15.4x as the level in a sector or fiscal sell-off.

So what. A fair multiple somewhat above today's is defensible, which means the multiple is more likely to help than to hurt if the forecasts are delivered. A fair multiple of 32x would need a 20% margin and a sector re-rating, and neither is in our forecasts.

Counter-case to my view. I may be anchoring on a depressed two-year window. The ten-year history says that this business has been valued above 24x half the time, and if AI fears lift from services companies the whole range of multiples moves up.

What would change my view. Two consecutive halves of rising margin, with Products approaching a quarter of revenue, would make a multiple in the mid-20s my central case.

Versus the market. The market's implied fair multiple is about 20x. I am with the market, a little above it on the upside, and well below the guideline.

Conclusion. The guideline fair multiple is 32.2x, but my own view is that 19x to 21x is fair today, with about 24x reachable only once the margin rise has been shown.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C; I place it in the upper half because the memo's own fair multiple of 19-21x sits above today's 17.4-18.4x and the own-range reading is near cheap, but not higher because part of the cheapness is deserved (the ten-year range was set in the 2019-22 faster-growth, near-zero-rate regime, the margin is unproven) and the peer reading pulls the other way.

12. Total shareholder return

What the model shows. At the guideline multiple, and from the 1124p share price the model uses:

The multiple and earnings parts multiply, and dividends add. From today's 1090p, the same values per share give returns of about +129% and +179%.

What drives the model's return.

  • The multiple. The re-rating from 18.4x to 32.2x is a 75% uplift, and the model assumes it is complete by September 2027. Including its compounding with earnings, the re-rating supplies 94 of the 122 points at the first horizon and 113 of the 171 points at the second. Without the re-rating, the return is +28% and +58%.
  • Earnings. Two-year-forward EPS rises from about 61p (FY2028) to about 77p by September 2027 and to 91p (FY2031) by March 2029. Of the EPS growth from FY2028 to FY2031, about half is revenue at a constant margin, about a third is the rise in margin, and about a tenth is buybacks. Earnings are the part of the return our research supports. The revenue half is well backed for FY2028 and less so each year after, and the margin third rests on the staffing mix and on Products' cost base.
  • Dividends. 31p, 34p and 36p a share over the three years, covered about 1.7 times, from a company with no debt that has raised its dividend every year since listing.

Two cautions on reading the model's return.

  1. The horizons are the model's fixed columns. They are 18 months and three years from the last reported year-end, so they fall about 10 months and 2.4 years from today. The short first horizon is why the first annualised figure, +148%, is so large.
  2. The split flatters the earnings part. The split measures today's multiple on FY2028 earnings. On earnings dated two years from today, about 67p on our forecasts, the shares are on 16x to 17x. So about ten points of the +25% earnings contribution to September 2027 is the calendar catching up, and underlying earnings growth is nearer 14%.

The return at other multiples (my arithmetic on the model's earnings and columns).

The skew over a true 18 months, from 1090p (my arithmetic and probabilities).

Weighted, the 18-month return is about +13%, or 8% to 9% a year. The modal path is attractive, the weighted path is ordinary, and the gap between them is the lower tail in topic 9.

Counter-case. The guideline may be right and I may be too cautious: if the margin leg is delivered into a recovering sector, a re-rating toward the mid-20s would add 30 to 40 points to the return on the delivered path.

What would change my view. Margin evidence would raise both the earnings and the multiple at once. That is the reinforcing combination, and it is why the November 2027 and May 2028 results carry so much of the return.

Versus the market. The median broker target implies +16% over twelve months. On delivered forecasts I am above that, because I have FY2029 and FY2030 earnings above consensus. On a probability-weighted view I am close to it.

Conclusion. Two-thirds to three-quarters of the model's return of +122% and +171% is re-rating to the guideline multiple. The part our research supports is an earnings-led return of roughly 27% to 35% over 18 months if the forecasts are delivered, and about 13% when the weaker paths are weighted in.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. About +13% falls in the C band and maps to about 57; I move it down to 54 for the fat lower tail (a one-in-five chance of about -23%) and because the model's +122%/+171% rests almost entirely on a re-rating to 32.2x that the memo itself rejects, while the three-year check at an unchanged multiple (+58% delivered) supports the earnings-led modal path.

13. Summary conclusion

Kainos is a good business at the midpoint of an earnings step-up. The demand is real, contracted and shared across its market. The founder-led reset has captured that demand. The balance sheet and cash generation are strong. And the market already knows all of this. What the market has stopped forecasting is the margin. Our forecasts have the margin rising from FY2028, for reasons that are near-mechanical in the first year and that then depend on a staffing change the company has published and has carried out once before. The result is a gap to consensus that is modest, rests on one variable and arrives late: about 4% on FY2028 operating profit and 7% on FY2029.

Three things should stay in view.

  • The next six months are uninformative and lean slightly negative, because the second half is seasonally the weaker one and the first evidence on staffing comes in May 2027 at the earliest.
  • The lower tail belongs to one payer, the UK state, and has three dated triggers inside FY2028.
  • The model's very large return rests on a guideline multiple that I judge too high for this phase. On earnings alone, the delivered case returns about 30% over 18 months and the weighted case about 13%.

The practical shape of the case is a calendar. Each date either narrows the range of outcomes or leaves it wide.

When the skew becomes unusually positive. The skew becomes unusually positive once the contractor count is seen to have peaked and the fiscal dates have passed. It also becomes unusually positive at a share price that already discounts a public-sector pause, because history says such a pause would be temporary.

Sources of the visuals. Charts and tables marked FactSet or Master Dashboard are the default visuals built from model update 3 and its inputs. The other charts are drawn from figures stated in this memo. Basis of history. History in the default financial visuals is on FactSet's reported basis; forecasts are on the company's adjusted basis, so the step from the last actual year to the first forecast year can include a difference of basis.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
